questions.question: Why does knowing an Oil-and-Vinegar (OV) structure help you invert a quadratic map?
options: Fixing vinegar variables turns the remaining system into linear equations in the oil variables
Quadratic equations become linear if you evaluate them at enough random points
OV maps are always permutations, so you can invert them with a lookup table
OV maps are invertible because their Jacobian is always non-singular
questions.explanation: The trapdoor is that, once vinegar variables are fixed, no oil variable multiplies another oil variable, so the unknown oils appear linearly.

questions.question: For a quadratic map P over a field, what does the polar form P'(x,y)=P(x+y)-P(x)-P(y) represent?
options: A bilinear map derived from P’s quadratic part
The gradient (vector of partial derivatives) of P at x
A hash of x and y into the output field
A method to remove the vinegar variables from P
questions.explanation: For quadratic maps, this finite-difference expression cancels constants/linears and leaves a bilinear form.

questions.question: In an OV map that vanishes on the oil subspace O (i.e., P(o)=0 for all o in O), which terms must be absent from each polynomial?
options: Any term that contains only oil variables (constants, oil linear, and oil×oil terms)
All vinegar×vinegar terms, because they prevent solvability
All vinegar×oil terms, because they leak the oil space
All linear terms (both vinegar and oil), because polar forms require homogeneity
questions.explanation: To ensure P(o)=0 whenever the vinegar part is 0, every term must contain at least one vinegar variable.

questions.question: After fixing vinegar variables, what is the algebraic form of the signing step P(v+o)=t in the oil variables?
options: A linear system A·o=b over the field
A quadratic system that still requires Gröbner bases
A discrete logarithm problem in a finite group
A lattice closest-vector problem
questions.explanation: With no oil×oil terms, each equation becomes linear in the oil variables once vinegar is fixed.

questions.question: Why does the naïve OV/UOV signing equation tend to fail in the MAYO setting when o < m?
options: It becomes m linear equations in only o unknowns, so for random targets it is usually inconsistent
The polar form stops being bilinear when o < m
The field stops being a field when o < m
Verification requires inverting the public key, which is not possible when o < m
questions.explanation: With fewer unknown oils than equations, only a small fraction of targets can be hit for a given vinegar choice.

questions.question: What is the key purpose of the whipped map P*(x1,...,xk) in MAYO?
options: Increase the number of oil unknowns to k·o so the signing linear system becomes solvable with high probability
Make verification quadratic-time so it is harder to forge signatures
Eliminate the need for hashing the message to a target vector
Convert the scheme into a stateful signature to prevent replay
questions.explanation: Whipping up turns the signing problem into m linear equations in k·o unknowns while preserving a trapdoor structure.

questions.question: Which implementation detail is most likely to leak secret information via timing in a naïve OV/UOV/MAYO signer?
options: Branchy Gaussian elimination and variable number of restarts when a linear system has no solution
Using addition modulo p instead of bitwise XOR
Using JSON for test vectors instead of a binary format
Using Python instead of C
questions.explanation: Pivot search, row swaps, and retry loops can leak structure and internal state unless carefully hardened.

questions.question: In the lesson’s solver, what does it mean when solve_linear_system_modp(A,b,p) returns None?
options: The system is inconsistent (no solutions) over GF(p)
The solution exists but is not unique
The solver found multiple solutions and refused to choose one
The matrix A is square but has determinant 1
questions.explanation: None indicates a contradiction after elimination (a zero row with a nonzero RHS).
